Empirical Research Plan – “Do Temporary Destructive Shocks Permanently Change City Size?  Evidence from the Allied Bombing of Japan”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method:  Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event–study in calendar time and a dose–response (continuous-DID) specification.

Rationale  
• The war provides a sharply dated, plausibly exogenous, nationwide shock whose intensity varied greatly across cities.  
• We observe the same cities repeatedly before (1925-1940) and after (1947-1965).  
• DID makes minimal functional-form assumptions and can be transparently complemented by visual pre-trend checks.  
• Because intensity is continuous (e.g., % built-up area destroyed) rather than strictly binary, we will estimate both a binary DID (treated = “bombed ≥ median destruction among the 303 cities”) and a continuous DID (β measures effect per 10 percent­age-point additional destruction).  
• Event-study coefficients allow us to test the key identifying assumption (parallel trends) and to trace the shape of recovery.

Optional augmentation  
Endogenous targeting is a concern.  Where possible we instrument intensity with (i) minimum flying distance to the closest US-occupied Marianas air-base in 1945 and (ii) prevailing upper-air wind speed along the bombing route, both predetermined.  These IVs are only used as a robustness exercise; the core identification is DID.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Primary measure:  built_up_destroyed_i (percent of pre-war built-up area destroyed, 0–100, USSBS, 66 cities; for the wider 303-city sample we proxy with bldg_destroyed_pc).  
• Binary treatment:  Treated_i = 1 if built_up_destroyed_i ≥ median(USSBS) ≈ 47 %; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
• Cities with destruction < median (or zero for strict no-bomb cities).  
• For continuous specifications, all cities enter; the identifying variation is in intensity.

Treatment timing  
• Event date t = 1945 (bombing stops in August 1945; the next census is 1947).  
• Pre-periods: 1925, 1930, 1935, 1940.  
• Post-periods: 1947, 1950, 1955, 1960, 1965.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel pre-treatment trends.  
   Plausibility: Industrial expansion 1925-40 was economy-wide.  We will test in an event-study.

A2.  No differential anticipation.  
   Cities could not move capital or population out in anticipation of incendiary bombing campaigns that began only in March 1945.

A3.  No spillovers that violate SUTVA.  
   While refugees relocated temporarily, all Japanese cities faced nationwide rationing, black-outs, and post-war macro-policies.  We will show that excluding immediate neighbors of heavily bombed cities (Tokyo metro area, Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto) does not alter results.

A4.  Composition invariance.  
   Census definitions of city boundaries are constant over time (municipality codes unchanged in the Micro Statistics).  We will verify coding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Endogenous target selection – larger, faster-growing, industrial cities were more likely to be bombed.  
   • Mitigation: (i) Pre-trend tests; (ii) rich controls for 1940 population, manufacturing share, port status; (iii) IV using flight-distance & wind aloft.

T2.  Measurement error in destruction intensity (66-city USSBS subsample).  
   • Mitigation: (i) Show robustness on the full 303-city casualty/destruction proxies; (ii) use alternative binary cutoffs (25th, 75th percentiles).

T3.  Post-war reconstruction policy targeting the most damaged cities (endogenous post-treatment shocks).  
   • Mitigation: control for per-capita central‐government reconstruction grants (grants_pc_it) and interact them with post indicators; re-estimate on a sub-sample of cities receiving below-median grants.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # fast FE regressions + event study
library(modelsummary) # tables

# ---- 1. Load data ----
cities <- fread("japan_cities_1925_1965.csv")   # assume tidy format:
# city_id, year, pop, built_up_destroyed, bldg_destroyed_pc, deaths_pc,
# grants_pc, prewar_industry_share, port_dummy, distance_marianas, wind_speed

# ---- 2. Variable construction ----
cities[, ln_pop := log(pop)]
med_destr <- median(cities[built_up_destroyed > 0, built_up_destroyed], na.rm=TRUE)
cities[, treated := as.integer(built_up_destroyed >= med_destr)]
cities[, post := as.integer(year >= 1947)]
cities[, rel_year := year - 1945]   # for event study

# ---- 3. Basic DID (binary) ----
did_bin <- feols(ln_pop ~ treated*post | city_id + year, data=cities)
etable(did_bin, title="Binary DID: effect of bombing on log population")

# ---- 4. Continuous DID (dose response) ----
did_cont <- feols(ln_pop ~ post*built_up_destroyed | city_id + year,
                  data=cities)
etable(did_cont, title="Continuous DID: effect per 10pp destruction")

# ---- 5. Event-study (Sun & Abraham 2020) ----
cities[, cohort := fifelse(treated==1, 1945, 0)]  # all treated in same year
es <- feols(ln_pop ~ sunab(cohort, year) | city_id + year,
            data=cities[year >= 1930 & year <= 1965])
iplot(es, ref.line = 1940, xlab="Year", ylab="β_t")

# ---- 6. IV robustness: distance × wind ----
cities[, destr_hat := fitted(lm(built_up_destroyed ~ distance_marianas + wind_speed))]
iv <- feols(ln_pop ~ post*1 | city_id + year | post ~ destr_hat, data=cities)
etable(iv, title="2SLS DID using distance & wind as instruments")

# ---- 7. Save results ----
modelsummary(list(did_bin, did_cont, es, iv), output="results.docx")
```

Robustness examples (not shown in code block to save space):  
• Re-estimate after dropping Tokyo, Osaka, Hiroshima, Nagasaki.  
• Alternative treatment cut-offs (25th, 75th pct.).  
• Control for grants_pc_it, prewar_industry_share × year FE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (spatial equilibrium with mobile labor and capital) predicts that if only physical capital is destroyed, long-run population will recover once capital rebuilds; fundamentals (location, market access) did not change.  Therefore:

• Immediate post-war (1947) population in heavily bombed cities ↓ 20–30 % relative to controls (matches 50 % housing loss × elasticity ≤ 1).  
• Coefficients should attenuate toward zero by 1960–65.  I expect β_10yrs ≈ -0.05 log points (≈ 5 %), statistically indistinguishable from zero.

Thus, shocks largely temporary; rank reversion is strong.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Sharp, well-timed intervention (bombing ends 1945)………..1  
C2. Parallel pre-trends demonstrated in event study……………...1  
C3. No anticipation/confounding shocks in pre-period……………1  
C4. No inter-group spillovers violating SUTVA………………………0 .5 (possible refugee flows)  
C5. Stable composition & measurement of outcome………………1  

Total = 4.5 / 5 – identification appears credible, though spillovers warrant caution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
